body:
Meaning of nuclear fusion

Nuclear fusion is a nuclear reaction in which 2 light atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy when the total mass of the products is less than the total mass of the original nuclei.

An atomic nucleus contains positively charged protons and, except in ordinary hydrogen, neutrons. Protons in different nuclei repel one another because they carry the same positive electric charge. This repulsion is called the electrostatic or Coulomb barrier. For fusion to occur, the nuclei must approach closely enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them together.

Extremely high temperatures give the nuclei sufficient kinetic energy to overcome much of this repulsion. Quantum tunnelling also contributes to fusion. In laboratory fusion experiments, temperatures of approximately 100 million degrees Celsius or more may be necessary, depending on the fuel and confinement conditions.

Thermonuclear fusion is fusion made possible by the very high thermal energy of the reacting nuclei. The term refers to the physical process, not to a particular machine.

Hydrogen isotopes used as fusion fuels

An isotope is an atom of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. Hydrogen has 3 important isotopes:

Hydrogen isotopeProtonsNeutronsImportant property
Protium, 1H10Most abundant form of hydrogen
Deuterium, 2H or D11Stable isotope found in natural water
Tritium, 3H or T12Radioactive isotope used in proposed fusion fuel cycles

The deuterium-tritium reaction is especially important in current fusion research because it is easier to achieve at experimentally attainable temperatures than many other proposed fusion reactions.

In this reaction, 1 deuterium nucleus combines with 1 tritium nucleus to produce a helium-4 nucleus and a neutron. The total energy released is approximately 17.6 MeV, where MeV means million electron volts.

The helium-4 nucleus is also called an alpha particle. It carries approximately 3.5 MeV of the released energy. The neutron carries approximately 14.1 MeV. In a magnetic confinement device, the positively charged alpha particle can remain confined and contribute to plasma heating, whereas the electrically neutral neutron is not confined by the magnetic field.

Why energy is released

The combined mass of the helium nucleus and neutron is slightly smaller than the combined mass of the deuterium and tritium nuclei. This difference, called the mass defect, appears as released energy according to Einstein's mass-energy relationship:

E = Δmc2

Here, E is the released energy, Δm is the decrease in mass, and c is the speed of light in vacuum. Because c is extremely large, a small change in nuclear mass corresponds to a substantial amount of energy.

The underlying explanation involves nuclear binding energy. For light nuclei, fusion can form products that are more tightly bound per nucleon. The corresponding decrease in total mass releases energy.

Fusion in stars and on Earth

Fusion powers the Sun and other stars. In the Sun, the dominant process is a sequence of reactions called the proton-proton chain, through which hydrogen is ultimately converted into helium. The laboratory deuterium-tritium reaction is not the same sequence as the Sun's dominant fusion pathway.

The Sun maintains fusion through its enormous gravitational pressure and high central temperature. On Earth, scientists must create the necessary conditions using artificial heating and confinement systems.

Where fusion fuel comes from

Deuterium occurs naturally in water, including seawater. Tritium is radioactive and available in much smaller quantities. Future deuterium-tritium fusion systems are expected to require a method of producing tritium from lithium, using neutrons generated during fusion.

Lithium is therefore considered an important potential resource for future fusion fuel production, although lithium itself is not the fuel nucleus that undergoes the main deuterium-tritium reaction.

Fusion compared with fission

FeatureNuclear fissionNuclear fusion
Basic processA heavy nucleus splits into lighter nucleiLight nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei
Typical exampleSplitting of uranium-235Combination of deuterium and tritium
Energy sourceChange in nuclear binding energyChange in nuclear binding energy
Commercial electricityEstablished technologyStill under development
Important radiation concernRadioactive fission products and spent fuelFusion neutrons, tritium and activated materials

Both processes release nuclear energy, but their fuel requirements, reaction products and technological challenges differ. Deuterium-tritium fusion does not create the same mixture of fission products as a conventional fission reactor. However, fusion is not completely free from radioactive materials or radiation hazards: tritium is radioactive, and fusion neutrons can make some surrounding materials radioactive through neutron activation.

Prelims focus

  • Fusion combines light nuclei; fission splits heavy nuclei.
  • Deuterium contains 1 proton and 1 neutron; tritium contains 1 proton and 2 neutrons.
  • Deuterium is stable, whereas tritium is radioactive.
  • Deuterium-tritium fusion produces helium-4 and a neutron, releasing about 17.6 MeV.
  • The Sun is powered by nuclear fusion, not ordinary chemical combustion.
  • Trap: Fusion produces fewer conventional fission products but is not free from radiation-related challenges.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, section 4.6, printed pp. 52-53; NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2021-22 edition, Chapter 14, Sources of Energy, section 14.3.4 and Nuclear Fusion box, printed pp. 251-252; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 34-35; ITER Organization, What Is Fusion? and Frequently Asked Questions, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Nuclear Fusion: How Light Nuclei Release Energy

body:
Why fusion requires plasma confinement

At extremely high temperatures, ordinary gas becomes a plasma, a state of matter containing free electrons and positively charged ions. Plasma is often described as the fourth state of matter, after solids, liquids and gases.

Fusion requires nuclei to approach one another with sufficient energy and sufficient frequency. The practical problem is therefore not merely to create high temperature. Scientists must also keep the fuel together long enough for fusion reactions to occur.

The 3 main conditions are:

  • High temperature: nuclei must move with enough energy to approach one another despite electrical repulsion.
  • Adequate particle density: enough reacting nuclei must be present for useful numbers of collisions.
  • Sufficient confinement time: energy and fuel must remain in the reacting region long enough for fusion to occur.

These conditions are related. A very dense fuel may be confined for only a very short time, whereas less dense fuel generally requires longer confinement. This explains why magnetic and inertial fusion approaches use very different experimental arrangements.

Magnetic confinement fusion

Magnetic confinement uses magnetic fields to control the motion of electrically charged plasma particles. Since ions and electrons respond to magnetic fields, their movement can be guided so that the hot plasma remains largely separated from the surrounding chamber walls.

A tokamak is a magnetic confinement device with a torus-shaped, or doughnut-shaped, plasma chamber. Strong magnetic fields help confine the plasma, while additional systems heat it to fusion-relevant temperatures.

The magnetic fields do not act as a perfectly rigid container. Plasma can still lose energy, develop instabilities or encounter chamber surfaces. Preventing such losses is a major part of fusion research.

The stellarator is another magnetic confinement approach. It also uses magnetic fields to confine plasma, but its magnetic-field arrangement differs from that of a tokamak. ITER uses the tokamak approach.

Inertial confinement fusion

Inertial confinement fusion compresses a very small quantity of fuel extremely rapidly. Powerful laser beams, or other intense drivers, deliver energy to a tiny fuel capsule.

The outer material heats and moves outward, causing the remaining capsule to compress inward. This produces exceptionally high temperature and density for a very short interval. Fusion must occur before the compressed fuel expands and disperses.

In an indirect-drive laser arrangement, laser energy first produces X-rays inside a surrounding enclosure, and these X-rays compress the fuel capsule. In a direct-drive arrangement, laser beams illuminate the capsule more directly.

What the National Ignition Facility demonstrated

The National Ignition Facility (NIF), operated by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States, uses laser-driven inertial confinement.

On 5 December 2022, an NIF experiment delivered approximately 2.05 MJ of laser energy to a deuterium-tritium target and produced approximately 3.15 MJ of fusion energy. This established laboratory fusion ignition under NIF's target-energy definition.

That achievement is important because the fusion output exceeded the laser energy delivered to the target. However, the entire facility consumed substantially more energy than the laser energy delivered to the target. The experiment did not produce net electricity for a power grid.

Fusion ignition, target energy gain and commercial electricity generation are different achievements. A successful laboratory fusion reaction does not by itself establish a practical electricity-generating fusion power station.

What the 2 approaches have in common

Both approaches try to overcome the same fundamental obstacle: light nuclei repel one another electrically. Both must achieve sufficiently high temperature and suitable confinement conditions. Both must also address energy losses and the effects of energetic fusion products.

The principal difference is how the fuel is held together. Magnetic confinement controls a hot, comparatively dilute plasma using magnetic fields. Inertial confinement creates a very dense, short-lived fusion region through rapid compression.

Prelims focus

  • Plasma consists of charged ions and free electrons.
  • Fusion depends on temperature, particle density and confinement time.
  • A tokamak is a torus-shaped magnetic confinement device.
  • Inertial confinement uses rapid compression of a small fuel target.
  • NIF achieved its first laboratory ignition result on 5 December 2022.
  • Trap: NIF's target-level energy gain did not mean the facility generated net electricity.

[Sources: International Atomic Energy Agency, Fusion Energy, Magnetic Confinement Fusion and Inertial Confinement Fusion; ITER Organization, What Is a Tokamak? and Frequently Asked Questions; Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Achieving Fusion Ignition and National Ignition Facility Frequently Asked Questions, including the 5 December 2022 experiment; consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Plasma Confinement: Tokamaks and Inertial Fusion

body:
What is ITER?

ITER is a large international experimental fusion project being built at Saint-Paul-lez-Durance in southern France. Its central experimental device is a tokamak intended to demonstrate important scientific and technological conditions needed for future fusion power plants.

ITER has 7 Members: the European Union, China, India, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Russia and the United States. India participates in the project through its national fusion research and industrial contributions.

ITER is not a commercial power station. It is designed to investigate whether a large, magnetically confined fusion plasma can produce substantially more fusion power than the external heating power supplied directly to the plasma.

ITER's planned fusion performance

ITER's principal deuterium-tritium fusion target is approximately 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of externally supplied plasma-heating power, corresponding to a plasma fusion gain factor of Q = 10. The design aims to sustain this performance in long pulses of approximately 400-600 seconds.

The gain factor is defined conceptually as the ratio of fusion power released in the plasma to external heating power delivered to the plasma. It does not include all the electricity consumed by the installation.

ITER will not generate electricity for the grid. Its proposed 500 MW is fusion thermal power, not electrical output. The 500 MW and Q = 10 figures are research targets, not results already achieved by ITER.

ITER also aims to study the production and control of a burning plasma, in which a large share of the plasma heating comes from energetic helium nuclei produced by fusion itself. These positively charged alpha particles remain influenced by the confining magnetic field and can transfer energy to the surrounding plasma.

ITER schedule and construction status

The following dates describe the project's published Baseline 2024 planning approach and construction information available at the 16 November 2026 content cutoff. Planned dates are not completed achievements.

  • 2005: France was selected as the project site.
  • 2006: The ITER Agreement was signed.
  • 2024: An updated baseline approach was reviewed, and its overall approach was approved by the ITER Council.
  • 28 July 2026: Installation of the sixth of 9 tokamak sector modules was completed, bringing approximately 2-thirds of the toroidal core into place at that milestone.
  • 2 October 2026: Delivery of the final vacuum-vessel sector brought all 9 vacuum-vessel sectors to the ITER site. Delivery to the site is different from installation inside the tokamak.
  • 2034: Start of Research Operation is the published planning target.
  • 2039: Start of the deuterium-tritium operation phase is the published planning target.

These schedules may change as construction, commissioning, safety review and experiments progress. In particular, the earlier 2025 First Plasma target belonged to a superseded planning approach and must not be treated as the operative 2026 schedule.

Why fusion electricity is technologically difficult

Fusion is scientifically established, but using it to provide reliable electricity requires several challenges to be solved together.

Maintaining a suitable plasma

The plasma must remain hot and sufficiently well confined. Turbulence, instabilities and energy losses can reduce performance. Strong heating and careful control are therefore necessary.

Obtaining enough tritium

Tritium is radioactive, scarce and difficult to store and handle. A future fusion system would need a dependable tritium supply. One proposed approach is to use fusion neutrons to produce tritium from lithium. ITER plans to test aspects of this concept through tritium-breeding test blanket modules.

Protecting materials from neutrons

The energetic neutrons from deuterium-tritium fusion can damage materials and cause neutron activation, making some materials radioactive. Materials must withstand these effects while remaining suitable for long-term service.

Moving beyond a successful experiment

Future power plants must be able to sustain appropriate fusion conditions, handle released energy and operate reliably. Achieving a high plasma gain in an experiment is one important step, but it is not equivalent to demonstrating a working commercial power station.

Gujarat's connection: Institute for Plasma Research

The Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) is located at Bhat, near Indira Bridge, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It is an aided institute of the Department of Atomic Energy and carries out research in plasma physics, magnetic confinement and fusion-related technologies.

Its major experimental facilities include:

  • ADITYA-U: the upgraded form of ADITYA, India's first indigenously developed tokamak. It is used for experiments involving plasma behaviour and control.
  • SST-1: India's first superconducting tokamak, developed to investigate long-duration plasma operation.

ITER-India is associated with IPR and coordinates important Indian contributions to ITER. This provides a direct Gujarat connection to international fusion research.

Prelims focus

  • ITER is an international tokamak experiment located in southern France.
  • India is 1 of ITER's 7 Members.
  • ITER's design target is 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of external plasma heating, giving Q = 10.
  • ITER is not designed to supply electricity to the grid.
  • IPR is located at Bhat, Gandhinagar; its tokamaks include ADITYA-U and SST-1.
  • Trap: The published 2034 and 2039 milestones are planned dates, not achievements already completed.

[Sources: ITER Organization, Facts and Figures, What Will ITER Do?, ITER in a Few Lines, and Project Progress in Milestones; ITER Organization, 38th ITER Council Meeting press release, 26 June 2026, and Two-thirds of ITER Tokamak Core Now in Place, 29 July 2026; Institute for Plasma Research, About Us and Research Facilities, sections on ADITYA-U and SST-1; consulted 16 November 2026. Construction status period: July-October 2026. Schedule status: Baseline 2024 approach reported at the 16 November 2026 cutoff.]
